row.note: Psalm 1 calls the wicked wind-driven chaff; that makes the commentary’s 87:5 debris a human moral image as well as dead vegetation, set against the righteous tree.
The commentary places 87:5’s spent pasture opposite 87:17’s good and abiding lot; Psalm 1’s planted tree bears fruit and its leaf does not wither.
Isaiah says all flesh is grass and its beauty a field flower; this gives the pasture’s decay in 87:5 a direct image of mortal transience.
After grass and flower fade, Isaiah says God’s word stands forever; beside 87:6’s promised recitation and 87:17’s abiding good, the contrast joins fading growth to enduring revelation.
The psalmist says there is none in heaven besides God and nothing on earth he desires; this is a concrete preference for God over earthly life and goods.
When flesh and heart fail, God remains the psalmist’s portion forever; that makes 87:17’s better, more lasting share a personal trust rather than a material asset.
The rich person takes nothing when he dies; the verse sharply limits the value of the worldly goods preferred in 87:16.
The heavens and earth wear out and change, while God remains the same; this gives 87:17’s permanence a creation-scale contrast.
Isaiah says earth and heavens pass while God’s salvation and righteousness endure; it closely frames the commentary’s contrast between transient dunya and what lasts.
Human days are like grass and a field flower that passes; this echoes 87:5’s pasture turned to debris and the commentary’s low valuation of worldly life.
Against the human flower that fades, the next verse says God’s steadfast love is everlasting; it supplies a specific enduring counterpart to the commentary’s 87:17.
In WLC numbering (English Malachi 4:1), the coming day makes the arrogant and evildoers stubble consumed by fire; it links discarded vegetation with the fate of the rejected.
God says he will smelt away Zion’s dross; this gives the commentary’s “chosen ones with no dregs” an interpretive counterpart in purification.
Ezekiel calls the house of Israel dross in a smelting furnace; unlike the commentary’s image of a low human class, the metaphor indicts a whole corrupt people as refuse.

Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life; it is a concrete scriptural choice of a life-giving course, though Deuteronomy frames it as covenantal life rather than the Qur’anic afterlife contrast.

Esau eats and sells his birthright, then the narrator says he despised it; the scene shows immediate bodily appetite displacing a more valuable inheritance, like the commentary’s critique of preferring the lower lot.

Amos tells Israel to hate evil, love good, and establish justice, with the hope that God may be gracious to Joseph’s remnant; this concretizes the commentary’s bakiyya as a moral remainder holding to goodness.
God preserves seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal; the faithful remnant gives a concrete Jewish-scriptural instance of the commentary’s people retaining their religion.
Daniel’s sleepers awake to everlasting life or everlasting disgrace; this directly supplies divergent lasting outcomes for the commentary’s better afterlife.
Qoheleth says humans and animals share the same fate and all return to dust; this resists reading mortal life as a route to distinct postmortem destinies.
Qoheleth asks who knows whether the human spirit goes upward and the animal spirit downward; the question expressly leaves uncertain the afterlife distinction asserted by 87:17.
Qoheleth says the dead know nothing and have no further reward; this is a direct countervoice to the commentary’s claim that the afterlife is the better, more abiding lot.

Proverbs says a little with righteousness is better than great revenues with injustice; it qualifies the commentary’s lexicon note that wealth merits “good” only when abundant and from a clean source by making integrity outweigh abundance.
The psalm says the righteous person’s little is better than the abundance of many wicked; it joins “better” to clean moral source while reversing the lexicon’s emphasis on plenty.
Avot calls this world an antechamber before the world to come and urges preparation for the banquet hall; it makes the commentary’s worldly/afterlife contrast a practical choice of where to prepare.

row.basis: better hour in world to come
row.note: Avot says an hour of bliss in the world to come is better than the whole life of this world; this directly states the comparison in 87:16–17, while also valuing repentance and good deeds in this life.
One son refuses the king’s terms and trusts the King of the universe to raise him to renewed life; fidelity is chosen over a threatened present life for enduring life.
A brother says he prefers death at human hands while relying on God to raise him; his choice under pressure resembles the commentary’s contrast of temporal life and a better lasting future.
The surviving brother contrasts brief suffering with the brothers’ share in ever-flowing life; it makes the temporal-versus-abiding comparison explicit.
The souls of the righteous are in God’s hand and are at peace despite seeming lost; this answers the commentary’s debris/forgetting side with what remains secure before God.
Though the righteous seem punished and dead, their hope is full of immortality; this gives 87:17’s lasting good a specific postmortem sense.
John’s winnowing image gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff; it directly joins the commentary’s debris image to a separation of lasting good from refuse.
Luke’s parallel report likewise gathers wheat and burns chaff; its own version makes the commentary’s sorting of selected and discarded outcomes eschatological.
At harvest the weeds are gathered and burned while wheat is stored; the parable gives the commentary’s “selection” a concrete scene of separating what is retained from what is discarded.
The net’s good fish are kept in vessels and the bad thrown away; this closely matches the commentary’s selected, dreg-free lot versus discarded residue.
The Son of Man separates all nations as a shepherd separates sheep and goats; this makes the commentary’s two lots a final moral sorting of people.
The separated groups go to eternal punishment or eternal life; it gives concrete lasting consequences to the selection scene.
Jesus warns that earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth and corrosion; this explains why the life and goods preferred in 87:16 cannot be the abiding good of 87:17.
Jesus instead directs disciples to treasure in heaven where it is not destroyed; this supplies a specific enduring alternative to earthly preference.
Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one’s life; this directly rebukes the preference for worldly life in 87:16.
Jesus says Mary chose the good portion that will not be taken from her; it combines choosing what is better with its permanence, as in 87:17.
God tells the prosperous barn-builder that his life is demanded that night; this exposes the fragility of the worldly accumulation preferred in 87:16.
Jesus concludes that the one who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God is a fool; the contrast gives moral content to what counts as good wealth.

Abraham tells the rich man he received good things in life while Lazarus received bad, but now Lazarus is comforted and he is in anguish; this is a concrete reversal of worldly valuation in the afterlife.

row.basis: life in this world versus eternal life
row.note: Jesus says the one who loves life in this world loses it, while the one who hates it keeps it for eternal life; this directly addresses the preference named in 87:16.
Paul counts all his former gains as loss and rubbish compared with gaining Christ; this makes the commentary’s debris image a deliberate revaluation of worldly status and profit.
Paul tells believers in humility to count others more significant than themselves; this is a concrete ethical use of the preference verb’s sense of putting another ahead of oneself.
Paul says not to look only to one’s own interests but also to those of others; it completes the commentary’s sense of īthār as preferring another over self.

Believers accept confiscation of property because they know they have a better and abiding possession; this nearly reproduces the commentary’s contrast between worldly goods and what is better and lasting.
Moses chooses mistreatment with God’s people over the temporary enjoyment of sin; this makes the choice against present worldly pleasure explicit.
Moses regards reproach as greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looks to the reward; the verse directly reorders worldly wealth by an enduring good.
Some tortured witnesses refuse release so they may obtain a better resurrection; this gives preference for the afterlife a concrete cost in present life.
The world and its desires pass away, but the one doing God’s will abides forever; this directly pairs 87:16’s worldly life with 87:17’s lasting alternative.
Peter quotes Isaiah’s grass and flower fading to describe all flesh; this brings the commentary’s pasture/debris image into an explicit contrast with permanence.
Peter applies Isaiah’s enduring word to the good news preached to his hearers; this Christian reading makes the commentary’s recitation in 87:6 an enduring proclamation amid fading life.
Paul contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal; this states the temporal/permanent valuation underlying 87:16–17.
Paul desires to depart and be with Christ because that is far better; it directly values the future with Christ above present life.
Paul says staying in the flesh is more necessary for the Philippians; read beside his desire to depart, this shows present life chosen for service to others rather than its own worldly advantage.
Paul tells the rich not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God; this sharpens the commentary’s question of which goods deserve to be preferred.
Rich believers are to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life; this connects wealth rightly used with a more enduring life.
James says the rich person will pass away like a field flower; the image echoes the commentary’s pasture that becomes debris and exposes worldly status as transient.
The next verse depicts the flower falling and its beauty perishing; it extends the specific fading-flower image against the permanence of 87:17.
Paul describes the fate of those who reject God as eternal destruction; this is a contrary lasting outcome to the good and abiding afterlife in 87:17.
Paul contrasts durable building materials with wood, hay, and straw; this gives the commentary’s distinction between selected quality and debris a testable image of works.
Each person’s work is revealed and tested by fire; beside 87:5’s debris and 87:17’s better lasting lot, the verse makes the sorting depend on what endures the test.
A household contains gold and silver vessels as well as wooden and earthen ones, some for honor and some for dishonor; this is a concrete image of differentiated worth rather than a shared story.
The one who cleanses himself becomes a vessel set apart for honorable use; this adds purification to the commentary’s image of selecting what contains no dross.

row.basis: this world and the next as opposed masters
row.note: The homily says the present and coming worlds are enemies and asks what profit is gaining the whole world while losing one’s soul; it turns the commentary’s choice into an explicit refusal to serve both.

row.basis: Martha’s present service and Mary’s lasting portion
row.note: Augustine reads Martha’s activity as the present life and Mary’s contemplation as the life to come; this interprets Luke’s portion “not taken away” as the permanent good over the present age.
Chrysostom reads Jesus’ contrast between earthly and heavenly treasure as a call to give wealth to the poor; this makes the commentary’s choice of the better good an ethical use of possessions.

Zephaniah says God leaves a humble and lowly people who take refuge in him; this unites the commentary’s “low” valuation and its bakiyya that still has religious substance, reversing any equation of low social standing with refuse.
The remnant of Israel speaks no lies and does no injustice; this makes the commentary’s morally intact remainder concrete, rather than treating what remains as mere debris.
The midwives fear God and refuse Pharaoh’s order to kill the Hebrew boys; this is a specific biblical choice of divine allegiance over a threatening ruler’s power in this life.

In WLC numbering (English Exodus 8:19), Pharaoh’s magicians call the plague “the finger of God” but remain in the Egyptian narrative without the Qur’anic magicians’ explicit refusal of Pharaoh and acceptance of death; the difference sharpens the commentary’s choice-under-threat scene.

The three Judeans say they will not serve the king’s gods even if God does not rescue them; this is another concrete choice of fidelity over threatened present life, like the magicians in the commentary’s cited Qur’anic scene.
Moses is told to write and teach a song for Israel and put it in their mouths; this connects 87:6’s divinely given recitation with a text deliberately made memorable across generations.
The song will not be forgotten from descendants’ mouths even amid calamity; this is a concrete scriptural counterpoint to 87:6’s promise that the prophet will not forget recitation.

The commentary labels Arabic نسي (n-s-y) in 87:6; Hebrew נשה (n-š-h), in Joseph’s “God made me forget” name explanation, is a related weak-root form. Here forgetting is relief from past hardship, unlike the Qur’anic promise of retained recitation.

The commentary’s form ٱلْءَاخِرَة (al-ākhirah) and Hebrew אַחֲרִית (ʾaḥarit), “future/outcome,” reflect the cognate Semitic root ʾ-ḥ-r/ʾ-kh-r; Proverbs uses it for the wise person’s hoped-for future, not unambiguously for a postmortem realm.
Proverbs calls a little with fear of the LORD better than great treasure with turmoil; this gives the commentary’s “good” wealth a moral condition and contests abundance as the measure of worth.
Proverbs says it is better to be lowly among the poor than share spoil with the proud; this reverses the commentary’s low/dunyā pole by making low social position preferable to proud worldly gain.
A good name is to be chosen over great riches, and favor over silver and gold; this directly joins the commentary’s language of choosing to a reordering of material value.

Proverbs says wealth acquired by vaporous means dwindles while gradual gathering grows; this adds a concrete warning about the source and durability of the wealth discussed in the commentary’s khayr gloss.
The psalmist delights in God’s statutes and says he will not forget the word; it gives a human devotional counterpart to 87:6’s promised retention of recitation.

row.basis: forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
row.note: Israel must leave a forgotten sheaf for the immigrant, orphan, and widow; what is accidentally left behind becomes provision for low-status people, qualifying the commentary’s image of discarded residue as worthless.

row.basis: field edge reserved for the poor
row.note: The harvest is not to be cut to the edge, and gleanings are left for the poor and immigrant; this gives “what remains” an ethical use rather than the contemptuous sense of dregs.

Qoheleth urges enjoyment of life with one’s spouse during one’s fleeting days under the sun; this is a specific counter-valuation of present life alongside the commentary’s preference for the afterlife.
Avot asks who is rich and answers: one who rejoices in his portion; this interprets wealth through contentment rather than the commentary’s lexicon note about material abundance.

The Mishnah says loving-kindness and honoring parents yield fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come; its opening discussion of field-corner gleanings also makes a deliberately retained remnant fruitful rather than refuse.
Jesus sets a broad way leading to destruction against a narrow way; this makes the commentary’s choice between the lower and better lot a concrete decision with opposed ends.
The narrow way leads to life and is found by few; it adds the positive outcome to the two-way choice that 87:16–17 presents.

Jesus says God clothes grass that is alive today and thrown into the oven tomorrow; unlike the commentary’s use of spent pasture as a figure of the low lot, the image argues that even transient grass is cared for and grounds trust.
Jesus tells the rich inquirer to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow him for treasure in heaven; this makes the better, lasting choice costly and relational.
The inquirer leaves grieving because he has many possessions; the narrative concretely shows worldly wealth winning out over the offered lasting good.
Jesus promises recognition to those who leave house, kin, or lands for him and the gospel; this gives a concrete cost to choosing the enduring good over present attachments.

row.basis: eternal life in the coming age
row.note: The promise culminates in eternal life in the coming age; this supplies the lasting outcome that frames the worldly losses of the preceding verse.
Jesus tells disciples to sell possessions and give alms, storing unfailing treasure in heaven; it joins the commentary’s selfless preference for others to its better, more lasting good.
Jesus says to invite the poor, disabled, lame, and blind rather than repayable guests; this enacts the commentary’s preference for another over oneself.
The host who cannot be repaid now will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous; it connects selfless preference with a future reward instead of worldly return.

row.basis: service to the least and the kingdom
row.note: The king identifies care for the least with service to himself; in the scene’s inheritance of the kingdom, this makes the commentary’s giving priority to another an act with lasting consequence.
The early community lays sale proceeds at the apostles’ feet and distributes to each as needed; this gives the commentary’s prefer-others sense a concrete communal practice.
The apostles answer threats by saying they must obey God rather than human authorities; this is a concise Christian parallel to choosing divine truth under worldly coercion.
Paul recalls Jesus’ saying that giving is more blessed than receiving; this directly illuminates the commentary’s definition of īthār as preferring another through generosity.

row.basis: Esau sells inheritance for one meal
row.note: Hebrews calls Esau profane because he sells his birthright for one meal; it interprets the Genesis scene as a choice of immediate appetite over inheritance.
Hebrews adds that Esau later seeks the blessing with tears but cannot reverse the outcome; this Christian reading stresses the lasting cost of choosing immediate appetite.
Hebrews says believers have no lasting city here but seek the one to come; it is an exact spatial formulation of preferring the abiding future to present worldly life.
Paul says the outer person is wasting away while the inner person is renewed day by day; this adds an inward, present renewal to the commentary’s contrast between decaying debris and abiding good.
Paul describes a remnant according to grace’s election; the verse joins the commentary’s retained bakiyya to its image of selecting the worthy lot.
James says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten; this concretely exposes the perishability of the goods preferred in 87:16.
Paul calls godliness with contentment great gain; this counters a material reading of “good” wealth by locating true gain in a moral disposition.
The teaching commands love for enemies and giving without demanding repayment; it turns the commentary’s preference for another over self into a specific Christian practice.
Clement recalls believers who sold themselves into slavery and used the price to feed others; this is an extreme concrete instance of preferring another’s need over one’s own freedom.

Thomas says one who knows the world has found a corpse and that the world is not worthy of that person; this is a specific, radical devaluation of the world alongside the commentary’s low/dregs imagery, though it does not itself state an afterlife contrast.
